five_point_argument: 1 LVT reduces vacancies (Harrisburg vacant lots -80%) [fn1 Library of Economic Possibility, Land Value Tax, 25 Feb 2023]

2 LVT raises amount and value of urban investment (Allentown building permits +32% [fn2: Progress LLM / progress.org wiki oates-schwab-pittsburgh page]; Pittsburgh +70% real value of permits 'while the LVT was still active' [fn3: Legalcamp blog, 18 Jul 2026])
3 equitable and relatively popular: many owners see decreases (Allentown 70% of residential parcels saw a decrease) [fn4: 'Id.' = Legalcamp blog]

4 secondary effects: Harrisburg crime -28%, 'thousands of new jobs', rated second-best US city to raise a family, once most distressed [fn5-7: Mark Alan Hughes, Why So Little Georgism in America, Lincoln Institute 2006]
5 revenue: taxes under-taxed vacant land, captures value from induced development (no figure; asserted)

pennsylvania_figures_and_sources_as_give.Harrisburg vacant lots -80%: Exec summary and 'Less speculation and blight' section: 'vacant lots dropped 80%' [fn1/fn30 Library of Economic Possibility]. The Harrisburg section of the same PDF instead says 'an 80% reduction in vacant structures' [fn69 = Hughes 2006]. Lots vs structures is an internal inconsistency in the brief.
pennsylvania_figures_and_sources_as_give.Harrisburg crime -28%: Hughes 2006 via fn5/fn69; also bullets: $4.8 billion investment, tax base $212 million to $1.6 billion, thousands of jobs. Adoption 1975; ratio 2:1 rising to 6:1; Stephen Reed credited (fn67 is a UBC student blog).
pennsylvania_figures_and_sources_as_give.Allentown permits +32%: Exec summary fn2 points to the progress.org wiki page for Oates-Schwab (a Pittsburgh study with no Allentown content); body (fn63) points to the Legalcamp blog. Citation does not support the figure as given.
pennsylvania_figures_and_sources_as_give.Allentown 70% of residential parcels pai: Legalcamp blog (fn4/fn62); adoption 1996 (fn60 StatesLaws). No primary source (no city or Pennsylvania DCED document, no Hughes page cite).
pennsylvania_figures_and_sources_as_give.Pittsburgh permit value +70%: Body names Oates & Schwab (National Tax Journal 50(1), 1997), says the authors did not claim the tax was the sole cause, notes Pittsburgh losing jobs/population, cites Plassmann & Tideman (2000) as reinforcing, and tells the 2001 repeal story (Wettick 1997 ruling, $23.9 million reassessment, botched assessments). But the footnotes route through the progress.org wiki summary (fn2, fn75) and Legalcamp (fn3), not the paper itself; the Exec Summary states the 70% without the caveats the body gives.

other_facts_in_pdf: Altoona: land tax adopted 2002, pure LVT 2011, abandoned 2016 (county and school district kept conventional taxes; public education lacking) [Altoona Mirror; FHWA]
Pennsylvania: 20 municipalities, 1913 enabling law; list of 19 names given
Four principles of an LVT system (flexible ratio, reassessment, existing exemptions apply, local autonomy) [fn3 Legalcamp]
Global list (Australia, NZ, Hong Kong, Singapore, Denmark, Estonia, Taiwan, England, Canada, Jamaica, Fiji, Kenya, South Africa) [Common Wealth Canada blog; McCluskey and Franzsen 2005]

State landscape 2026: Maryland two bills, DC act, Maine bill; Minnesota, New York, Ohio, New Hampshire enablement bills proposed; Michigan, Washington emerging; Kentucky and Virginia signed 2026 [Center for Land Economics tracker]
Gentrification protections listed (eviction protections, rent control, tenant co-ops, right-to-buy, subsidies, inclusionary zoning) [HHS ACF guide]
buffalo_specific_facts: 'around 15,300 total vacant lots', mostly East Side [fn8 Sam Magavern, Putting Vacant Land to Good Use, PPG Buffalo in Transition, 15 May 2025 - a named, checkable PPG report; not fetched]
'Buffalo already has an assessment system in place' [fn34 City of Buffalo 2026 Final Assessment Roll on OpenData Buffalo; the brief offers no assessment-practice detail beyond that sentence]

February 2023: Council Member Golombek discussed LVT and the Common Council 'unanimously adopted a resolution that would research the pros and cons' [fn20 PPG Common Council summary week of 20 Feb 2023; fn21 Buffalo Rising]
New York: 'a bill in a Senate Committee' enabling local LVT [fn19 S1131B, 2025-26]. No mention of Erie County. The brief does not mention New York's 2026 Section 119-r renewal.
Oates-Schwab 15-city sample 'included Buffalo' (true per the wiki's own note on city samples), Buffalo being a comparison city that saw no/declining construction
content_summary.proposed_next_steps: No formal proposal (no bill, pilot, or ordinance text). Conclusion: Buffalo should 'strongly consider' LVT; use a third-party assessment to avoid political pressure; inform the public that LVT would lower most homeowners' taxes.

No places/new-york-state, no Buffalo page; places/new-york-city.md is NYC-only; events/2026-state-lvt-enablement-wave.md covers NY (Section 119-r renewal; S1131B dead as of 5 Jun 2026) and lists Minnesota only among stalled bills. Buffalo appears in the wiki only incidentally (Oates-Schwab sample, LOOPLOG).

title: Seeds from Henry George
what_was_fetched: Full page, HTTP 200 (226 KB HTML; article text about 1,500 words). Saved: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-georgism-wiki/27113c0d-0e4a-5705-a87d-69e4d8108829/scratchpad/t0-2026-11-10/item2-seeds-text.txt and /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-georgism-wiki/27113c0d-0e4a-5705-a87d-69e4d8108829/scratchpad/t0-2026-11-10/item2-seeds-page.html. No PDF. No access failures. Page header reads: 'The Gardener's Guide - Part 2 - Chapter 1 of 4'; byline 'By John Emmeus Davis - Illustrations by Bonnie Acker - 2014'. Chapters of the series listed as Domestic Pioneers: Seeds from Henry George, School of Trustery, The Small Community, The Koinonia Connection.
verdict: ENRICH concepts/community-land-trust.md (Origins section): add one or two sentences giving the Georgist lineage as Davis states it (Henry George and the single tax; the single-tax colonies Fairhope 1894 and Arden 1900, Arden with 99-year ground leases; Lincoln benefaction), attributed to Davis. Optional second sentence on organizations/fairhope-single-tax-corporation.md only if it adds something the page lacks (it already has 1894 and 99-year leases, so probably NOT needed). Do not state that the CLT 'took the lease and dropped the tax' as Davis's claim - he does not say it.
claim_grade: A/B for the narrative of lineage (a recognised scholar and editor of The Community Land Trust Reader, Lincoln Institute 2010; Tier 1 by the 4c rubric - Davis is not listed in sources/audit/people-tiers.json, so the rubric applies; the host is the sector's own International Center for Community Land Trusts, an institutional resource). Interpretive 'George's legacy to the CLT movement' is the author's own framing - attribute it, do not assert it in the wiki's voice. The Lincoln Institute 1946 sentence is C (see uncertainties).

exact_wording_key_passages.thesis: The intellectual origins of the modern-day community land trust begin in the United States with a home-grown, self-educated political economist named Henry George.
exact_wording_key_passages.standfirst: The CLT's intellectual roots in the United States begin with Henry George, the self-taught economist who argued that rising land values belong to the community.
exact_wording_key_passages.mill: He was struck by Mill's concept of the "social increment," an economic theory asserting that most of the appreciating value of land is created not by the investment or labor of individual landowners, but by the growth and development of the surrounding society. (Davis uses 'social increment', not 'unearned increment'.)
exact_wording_key_passages.single_tax: Instead, he proposed a single tax: Have government tax away the social increment, collecting for the benefit of the public all of the land gains that society itself has created.
exact_wording_key_passages.progress_and_poverty: He laid out his argument for the single tax in Progress and Poverty, published in 1879. His book was a bestseller. ... spawning an international "single-tax movement."
exact_wording_key_passages.colonies: Back in the United States, other followers of Henry George were busily developing experimental communities of their own. These so-called "single-tax colonies" combined community ownership of the land and individual ownership of the structural improvements. The first was established in Fairhope, Alabama in 1894 on the eastern shore of Mobile Bay.
exact_wording_key_passages.arden: Another single-tax colony was established in Arden, Delaware in 1900, outside of Wilmington. The founders drew up plans for a village of artists and artisans, where the land would be held in trust. Residents were granted 99-year ground leases. They could sell their houses but not the land. Upon the resale of a house, the land lease was transferred to the new homeowner. ... a thriving community that still exists, a hundred years later. Its current population is over 500 people.
exact_wording_key_passages.lincoln: Another part of George's legacy to the CLT movement is the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy. The Institute was established in 1946 by John C. Lincoln, a Cleveland industrialist and investor. He was intrigued by the writings of Henry George, especially George's ideas about land ownership and taxation. Lincoln created the Foundation to support other institutions in the teaching, research, and publication of information about George's work.
exact_wording_key_passages.lincoln_funding: In 2005, under the leadership of Roz Greenstein, the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy stepped in to provide critical financial and logistical support for the National CLT Conference in Portland, Oregon ... One year later, Lincoln underwrote the creation of the National CLT Academy ... during the six-year span of the Academy's operation.

content_summary.what_davis_does_not_say: He does not discuss what the CLT took from George versus what it dropped; there is no tax-versus-lease or community-ownership-versus-single-tax-theory analysis on this page. His only explicit contrast is descriptive: Henry George rejected nationalisation and proposed the single tax; the colonies 'combined community ownership of the land and individual ownership of the structural improvements'. Ralph Borsodi, the School of Living and Robert Swann are NOT mentioned on this page (they belong to the next chapter, 'School of Trustery', not fetched). Fairhope is mentioned only for date and place; no 99-year lease statement for Fairhope on this page (99-year ground leases are stated for Arden). Key-dates box: 1894 Fairhope, 1900 Arden, 1925 Robert Schalkenbach Foundation, 1946 Lincoln Institute. Further reading includes Henry Wiencek, 'A Delaware Delight: The Oasis Called Arden', in Davis (ed.), The Community Land Trust Reader (Lincoln Institute 2010).

existing_wiki_coverage: concepts/community-land-trust.md Origins section already dates the CLT to New Communities Inc. (1969) and names Borsodi and Swann's International Independence Institute, then says: 'The deeper lineage reaches back through Ebenezer Howard's garden cities and the single-tax colonies like Fairhope, which pioneered community land ownership funded by ground rents.' It has no mention of Davis, George-to-CLT lineage per Davis, Mill, Arden's 99-year leases, or Lincoln. Its 'Relation to Georgism' section frames the CLT as 'a cousin of Georgism, not a copy of it' (tax versus decommodifying lease), which is the wiki's own synthesis, uncited to Davis. Sources already cite cltweb.org only for the New Communities page [2]. organizations/fairhope-single-tax-corporation.md already has 1894, 99-year renewable leases, and one sentence on Arden (founded 1900 by Frank Stephens and Will Price); it links to the CLT page as 'modern nonprofit analogue'. events/single-tax-colonies.md exists (Fairhope and Arden). organizations/lincoln-institute.md states 'founded: 1946' and 'traces its mission to the ideas of Henry George via its founder, John C. Lincoln'. No Borsodi, Swann, Arden or School of Living page in the digest (digest has events/single-tax-colonies, organizations/lincoln-institute, concepts/garden-city-movement, books/genovese-earth-for-all).
anchor_sentence_for_enrich: Exact current text, concepts/community-land-trust.md, end of Origins paragraph: "The deeper lineage reaches back through [Ebenezer Howard's](/wiki/ebenezer-howard/) garden cities and the [single-tax colonies](/wiki/single-tax-colonies/) like [Fairhope](/wiki/fairhope-single-tax-corporation/), which pioneered community land ownership funded by ground rents." (the sentence wraps across three lines in the file: 'The deeper lineage reaches back through [Ebenezer / Howard's](/wiki/ebenezer-howard/) garden cities and the [single-tax / colonies](/wiki/single-tax-colonies/) like [Fairhope](/wiki/fairhope-single-tax-corporation/), / which pioneered community land ownership funded by ground rents.'). Suggested insertion directly after it, in the wiki's impersonal voice, e.g.: 'John Emmeus Davis, the leading historian of the movement, traces the CLT's intellectual origins to Henry George and John Stuart Mill's "social increment", through the single-tax colonies at Fairhope (1894) and Arden (1900), where residents held 99-year ground leases and could sell their houses but not the land.' uncertainties: SCANNER PREMISE CHECK: (a) 'Borsodi and the School of Living if mentioned' - not mentioned on this page. (b) 'Robert Swann' - not mentioned. (c) 'what the CLT took from George and what it dropped (the tax vs the lease)' - Davis does not make this comparison; any such sentence would be the wiki's own synthesis, which the page already has in 'Relation to Georgism'. Do not repeat '1946 Institute' on Davis's authority without checking the Institute's own history page; the Georgist-lineage sentence needs only 'John C. Lincoln, an industrialist influenced by George, endowed the foundation from which the Institute grew' if at all.
